case_analysis.focal_point: Whether U.S. courts may exercise subject-matter jurisdiction under the FSIA’s expropriation exception over Holocaust-era property claims against Hungary (and related entities), including how the domestic-takings rule (as clarified in Philipp) and jurisdictional pleading/proof standards apply at the motion-to-dismiss stage.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act (FSIA), chiefly 28 U.S.C. § 1605(a)(3) (the expropriation exception), along with related FSIA jurisdictional provisions (e.g., 28 U.S.C. § 1330; immunity framework in 28 U.S.C. §§ 1602 et seq.).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Hungary argues the suit is barred by sovereign immunity because the plaintiffs’ allegations do not satisfy the FSIA expropriation exception as properly construed—particularly after the Supreme Court’s clarification in Philipp that a foreign sovereign’s taking of its own nationals’ property is a domestic taking and is not a taking 'in violation of international law' for purposes of § 1605(a)(3). Hungary also presses procedural/jurisdictional objections about what plaintiffs must plausibly plead and ultimately prove to establish the exception, urging dismissal (at least for plaintiffs who were Hungarian nationals at the time of the alleged takings) and a narrower approach to allowing jurisdictional discovery or merits litigation to proceed.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The plaintiffs (Holocaust survivors and heirs) contend the case fits within the FSIA expropriation exception and should not be dismissed at the pleading stage; they maintain their allegations are sufficient to invoke an immunity exception and that the complex procedural history (including vacaturs and remands) does not foreclose their ability to proceed. They also argue that, even under intervening precedent like Philipp, at least some plaintiffs and/or theories remain viable and that disputed factual issues (e.g., nationality at the time of taking, how the taking is characterized, and the required commercial-activity nexus) should not be resolved against them on a motion to dismiss.
key_precedents: Republic of Hungary v. Simon (procedural posture reflected in the Simon line of decisions: Simon-2014; Simon I; Simon-2017; Simon II; Simon-2020)
Federal Republic of Germany v. Philipp ("Philipp")
Belize Social Development Ltd. v. Government of Belize, 794 F.3d 99 (D.C. Cir. 2015)
Phoenix Consulting, Inc. v. Republic of Angola, 216 F.3d 36 (D.C. Cir. 2000)
United States v. Munsingwear, Inc., 340 U.S. 36 (1950)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s proposal for targeted jurisdictional discovery is the strongest counter, but it presupposes that plaintiffs have plausibly alleged facts bringing the case within § 1605(a)(3) in the first place; discovery cannot be used to search for an exception when the pleadings (or undisputed materials) indicate Hungarian nationality at the time of the taking, which Philipp makes dispositive under the domestic-takings rule. Philipp’s remand for nationality determinations supports a limited, fact-bound inquiry only where there is a genuine, plausibly pleaded dispute—not a license to let conclusory allegations proceed to merits-stage burdens on a foreign sovereign. As Justice Alito notes, Phoenix Consulting reinforces that FSIA immunity is jurisdictional and courts must resolve threshold disputes early, with any discovery tightly cabined to jurisdictional facts rather than allowing litigation to bootstrap jurisdiction. A narrow, institutionally modest disposition—dismiss domestic-takings-barred claims while permitting only adequately pleaded non-domestic takings theories to proceed through ordinary FSIA gatekeeping—best fits our precedents and preserves legitimacy.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s argument for targeted jurisdictional discovery is the best counter, but it cannot displace the FSIA’s text: immunity is jurisdictional and the plaintiff must plead facts bringing the case within § 1605(a)(3) before the sovereign is subjected to litigation. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Alito emphasize, Phoenix Consulting contemplates resolving genuinely disputed jurisdictional facts early; it does not authorize merits discovery to search for a jurisdictional hook when the complaint fails plausibly to allege non-Hungarian nationality. Philipp makes nationality at the time of taking a gatekeeping fact because “taken in violation of international law” incorporates the domestic-takings rule, so conclusory reframing as genocide-related wrongdoing cannot supply jurisdiction. Limited jurisdictional discovery may be permissible only after a concrete, exception-specific, plausible allegation of non-national status creates a real dispute; otherwise dismissal is required for want of § 1330 jurisdiction.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point—that targeted jurisdictional discovery may be warranted when nationality is genuinely disputed—has force as a matter of procedural fairness, but it cannot displace the FSIA’s structure making immunity the baseline and § 1605(a)(3) the plaintiff’s burden at the threshold. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, Philipp treats nationality at the time of the taking as a jurisdictional gatekeeping fact under the domestic-takings rule; where the pleadings or undisputed materials indicate Hungarian nationality, there is no plausible “violation of international law,” and the court lacks jurisdiction to permit discovery aimed at creating it. Phoenix Consulting (and the D.C. Circuit’s related approach) supports cabining any jurisdictional discovery to cases where the complaint already plausibly alleges non-national status and the court needs limited facts to resolve a real jurisdictional dispute—not to let litigation proceed on speculation. I would therefore dismiss claims barred by the domestic-takings rule, with at most a narrow remand for any specifically pleaded, plausible non-Hungarian nationality theories and the statutory nexus.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I accept, as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, that Philipp makes nationality at the time of the taking a jurisdictional gatekeeping fact and compels dismissal of claims that are plainly domestic takings by Hungarian nationals. But I do not read Phoenix Consulting or Belize Social Development as requiring courts to resolve genuinely disputed nationality questions against plaintiffs on a sparse pleadings record; those cases permit jurisdictional fact-testing, and that can include tightly limited discovery where plaintiffs plausibly allege non-Hungarian status, denaturalization, or expatriation and the relevant records are uniquely in foreign hands. Justice Alito’s insistence on early resolution is right as a sequencing principle, yet it cuts in favor of targeted jurisdictional discovery to accurately resolve the immunity question—not categorical dismissal when the complaint concretely puts nationality in play and the dispute is fact-bound. Under a pragmatic FSIA approach attentive to access-to-justice concerns, I would enforce Philipp’s domestic-takings rule while allowing narrow remand for jurisdictional development only for plaintiffs who plausibly allege they were not Hungarian nationals at the time of the taking.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point—that courts should allow targeted jurisdictional discovery before resolving disputed nationality facts against survivors—has force as a matter of fair procedure, and Philipp’s own remand confirms nationality can be fact-intensive. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Alito emphasize, the FSIA makes immunity the baseline and § 1605(a)(3) an exception that plaintiffs must plausibly plead into; Philipp makes non-domestic-taking nationality status a jurisdictional gatekeeping fact, so discovery cannot be used to supply what the complaint fails to allege with exception-specific plausibility. Phoenix Consulting and Belize Social Development reinforce the sequencing: courts may permit limited jurisdictional discovery only to resolve a genuine, concretely framed jurisdictional dispute, not to allow open-ended merits discovery to bootstrap jurisdiction. A workable middle ground is dismissal where the pleadings/undisputed materials indicate Hungarian nationality, with remand only for narrowly tailored jurisdictional development where plaintiffs plausibly allege non-Hungarian status and identify specific factual gaps.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor rightly presses that courts should not resolve genuinely disputed jurisdictional nationality facts against survivors without some targeted discovery, especially where plaintiffs plausibly allege non-Hungarian status or denaturalization. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Alito emphasize, the FSIA’s text makes immunity the baseline and jurisdiction the exception, and Philipp makes nationality at the time of the taking a jurisdictional gatekeeping fact because § 1605(a)(3) incorporates the domestic-takings rule. Phoenix Consulting (and Belize Social Development) supports cabined, jurisdiction-focused procedures only after the complaint plausibly invokes an exception; it does not authorize discovery to search for a jurisdictional foothold when the pleadings themselves indicate a domestic taking. I therefore would dismiss claims where Hungarian nationality is apparent or not plausibly negated, while allowing narrowly tailored jurisdictional development only for specifically pleaded, non-domestic-taking theories on remand.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right that, in an appropriate case, narrowly tailored jurisdictional discovery can be a fair tool to resolve genuinely disputed nationality questions, especially where the pleadings plausibly allege non-Hungarian status and the facts are uniquely in the sovereign’s control. But as the Chief Justice (Roberts) and Justice Kagan emphasize, Philipp makes nationality at the time of the taking a jurisdictional gatekeeping fact for whether § 1605(a)(3) can apply at all, and Phoenix Consulting supports resolving FSIA jurisdictional issues early rather than allowing merits discovery to bootstrap jurisdiction. Institutionally and administratively, we should require a plausible, exception-specific allegation of non-domestic taking (including non-national status) before any discovery, while leaving room on remand for limited jurisdictional development only where that threshold is met. That approach respects precedent, preserves the FSIA’s immunity-first structure, and avoids inviting foreign-relations friction through prolonged litigation where the statute and Philipp foreclose jurisdiction.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right that nationality can be fact-intensive and that targeted jurisdictional discovery may sometimes be appropriate, especially where plaintiffs plausibly allege denaturalization or non-national status and the relevant records are uniquely in the sovereign’s possession. But under Philipp the domestic-takings rule is embedded in the text of “taken in violation of international law” in § 1605(a)(3), making nationality at the time of the taking a jurisdictional gatekeeping fact; where the pleadings themselves indicate Hungarian nationality, a court lacks § 1330 jurisdiction and must dismiss rather than authorize discovery to pursue a legally foreclosed theory. Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on Phoenix Consulting (and Belize Social Development) reinforces that sequencing: FSIA immunity is immunity from suit, so courts must resolve threshold jurisdictional facts before imposing litigation burdens, with discovery—if any—tightly limited to genuine, specifically pleaded disputes. I therefore maintain that dismissal is required for claims that are domestic takings on the face of the pleadings, while leaving room on remand for narrowly cabined jurisdictional development only where non-national status is plausibly and concretely alleged.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s fairness-based push for targeted jurisdictional discovery has real force in cases involving vulnerable plaintiffs, and I agree that courts should not reflexively credit a sovereign’s nationality assertions where the complaint plausibly alleges non-national status. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Philipp makes the domestic-takings rule part of the § 1605(a)(3) “violation of international law” element and treats nationality at the time of taking as a jurisdictional gatekeeping fact; allowing discovery when the pleadings themselves fail to plausibly place non-Hungarian nationality in issue risks turning immunity from suit into a merits-screening device. Phoenix Consulting and Belize Social Development, invoked by Justice Alito, reinforce that sequencing: limited jurisdictional development can be appropriate to resolve a genuine, plausibly alleged dispute, but it cannot be used to fish for an exception where the complaint is jurisdictionally deficient. On a pragmatic, procedure-protective view, the administrable line is dismissal of domestic-takings-barred claims while permitting narrowly tailored jurisdictional inquiry only when plaintiffs concretely and plausibly plead facts suggesting non-domestic takings.

John Roberts.reasoning: Under the FSIA, plaintiffs bear the burden to plead facts bringing the case within an immunity exception, and at the motion-to-dismiss stage a court must ensure the § 1605(a)(3) elements are plausibly alleged (and may require proof if jurisdictional facts are genuinely disputed). Philipp unanimously reaffirmed the domestic-takings rule: a sovereign’s taking of its own nationals’ property is not “in violation of international law” for § 1605(a)(3), foreclosing jurisdiction at least for claimants who were Hungarian nationals at the time of the alleged takings. Consistent with institutional restraint and precedent, the proper course is a narrow remand/dismissal as to those claims barred by Philipp, rather than allowing broad merits discovery to proceed without a viable jurisdictional basis under §§ 1330 and 1605(a)(3). This approach respects the FSIA’s immunity framework while leaving room for any remaining claims (e.g., involving non-nationals at the time of taking, if adequately pleaded) to be evaluated under ordinary jurisdictional standards.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The FSIA’s expropriation exception applies only when “rights in property taken in violation of international law” are at issue, 28 U.S.C. § 1605(a)(3), and the original public meaning of that phrase incorporates the domestic-takings rule: a sovereign’s taking of its own nationals’ property is not a violation of international law. Federal Republic of Germany v. Philipp squarely rejected the attempt to evade that rule by recasting a domestic taking as genocide for § 1605(a)(3) purposes, and thus requires dismissal at least as to plaintiffs who were Hungarian nationals at the time of the alleged takings. Because FSIA immunity is jurisdictional, 28 U.S.C. § 1330, courts must insist at the motion-to-dismiss stage that plaintiffs plausibly allege facts bringing the case within § 1605(a)(3), including the necessary nationality allegations under Philipp, rather than allowing jurisdiction to rest on conclusory characterizations. To the extent the record cannot support that jurisdictional showing, the suit must be dismissed for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 1605(a)(3) requires property be “taken in violation of international law,” and Philipp reaffirmed the domestic-takings rule: a sovereign’s taking of its own nationals’ property is not within the expropriation exception, rejecting the attempt to recharacterize such takings as genocide-based violations for § 1605(a)(3) purposes. At the motion-to-dismiss stage, plaintiffs bear the burden to plead facts plausibly bringing their claims within an FSIA exception, and once immunity is challenged they must ultimately prove jurisdictional facts; D.C. Circuit cases like Phoenix Consulting emphasize courts must resolve FSIA jurisdictional disputes rather than allow speculative allegations to open-ended discovery. Given Philipp, claims by plaintiffs who were Hungarian nationals at the time of the alleged takings fall outside § 1605(a)(3), and prudentially the courts should not expand U.S. jurisdiction over foreign sovereigns absent clear statutory text, especially where doing so invites substantial foreign-relations friction. Accordingly, Hungary’s immunity should be respected at least to the extent the complaints do not plausibly allege non-domestic takings and the requisite statutory nexus.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: At the motion-to-dismiss stage, courts should require plaintiffs to plausibly allege facts bringing their claims within FSIA § 1605(a)(3), but not resolve genuinely disputed jurisdictional facts against Holocaust survivors without targeted jurisdictional discovery where appropriate (see Phoenix Consulting and Belize Social Development on jurisdictional pleading/proof burdens). Philipp confirms the domestic-takings rule: a sovereign’s taking of its own nationals’ property is not a taking “in violation of international law,” so claims by plaintiffs who were Hungarian nationals at the time of taking must be dismissed, but Philipp does not justify categorical dismissal of all claims where plaintiffs plausibly allege non-Hungarian nationality at the relevant time. Given the remedial purpose of the expropriation exception and the severe practical consequences of premature dismissal, jurisdiction should remain for those plaintiffs who plausibly plead non-domestic takings and the required nexus under § 1605(a)(3), with nationality determinations addressed on a fuller record. This approach respects sovereign immunity while preserving access to justice for vulnerable survivors where the statute plausibly applies.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 1605(a)(3) requires “rights in property taken in violation of international law,” and Philipp makes clear that the FSIA incorporates the domestic-takings rule: a sovereign’s taking of its own nationals’ property is not such a violation, even when the taking is alleged to be part of genocide. At the motion-to-dismiss stage, courts may look beyond bare allegations and require plaintiffs to plausibly plead facts showing the exception applies, including facts supporting non-national status at the time of the taking; D.C. Circuit FSIA practice likewise places on the plaintiff the burden to produce evidence once immunity is challenged (Phoenix Consulting; Belize Social Development). Because Philipp also remanded for consideration of nationality, it underscores that nationality is a jurisdictional gatekeeping fact for § 1605(a)(3), and absent plausible non-national allegations, Hungary retains immunity and the case should be dismissed (at least as to domestic-takings-barred claims). This approach maintains statutory coherence and administrable jurisdictional rules under § 1330 and the FSIA’s immunity framework.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The FSIA makes immunity the rule and jurisdiction the exception, and § 1605(a)(3) applies only when “rights in property [were] taken in violation of international law.” In Philipp, the Court held that this phrase incorporates the international law of expropriation and thus the domestic-takings rule, meaning a sovereign’s taking of its own nationals’ property is not “in violation of international law” for § 1605(a)(3) purposes, even when framed as part of genocide. At the motion-to-dismiss stage, plaintiffs must at least plausibly plead facts taking their claims outside that rule—most centrally, non-national status at the time of the taking (or some other basis within the expropriation exception’s text)—and courts should not expand jurisdiction by recharacterizing domestic takings as international-law violations contrary to Philipp and the FSIA’s separation-of-powers structure. Because Hungary’s immunity cannot be displaced on allegations that, under Philipp, amount to domestic takings by a sovereign from its own nationals, the suit should be dismissed at least as to those plaintiffs/claims.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: FSIA jurisdiction exists only if plaintiffs satisfy an immunity exception, and § 1605(a)(3) requires a taking “in violation of international law.” Under Federal Republic of Germany v. Philipp, a sovereign’s taking of its own nationals’ property is a “domestic taking” and does not qualify, so claims by plaintiffs who were Hungarian nationals at the time of the alleged expropriations must be dismissed for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction. Consistent with D.C. Circuit FSIA practice (e.g., Phoenix Consulting) and the statute’s jurisdictional structure (28 U.S.C. §§ 1330, 1602 et seq.), courts may resolve threshold nationality and exception-applicability issues at the motion-to-dismiss stage, permitting only limited jurisdictional discovery where genuinely necessary. Given the Court’s institutional interest in predictable, workable FSIA rules and adherence to precedent, the proper course is to enforce Philipp’s domestic-takings limitation and require plausible, exception-specific jurisdictional allegations before allowing the case to proceed.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The FSIA’s expropriation exception applies only when “rights in property taken in violation of international law are in issue,” 28 U.S.C. § 1605(a)(3), and under the domestic-takings rule a sovereign’s taking of its own nationals’ property is not such a violation. Federal Republic of Germany v. Philipp unanimously rejected the theory (embraced by the D.C. Circuit in Simon I) that characterizing a taking as part of genocide alone suffices to bypass the domestic-takings rule for § 1605(a)(3). At the motion-to-dismiss stage, plaintiffs must plausibly allege facts establishing an FSIA exception—and where the pleadings show the claim turns on domestic takings (e.g., plaintiffs were Hungarian nationals at the time), subject-matter jurisdiction is absent and dismissal is required rather than allowing merits litigation to proceed. Precedent thus requires a narrower jurisdictional approach here, at least as to plaintiffs whose claims fall within Philipp’s clarified domestic-takings rule.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Under the FSIA, subject-matter jurisdiction exists only if plaintiffs plausibly bring their claims within a statutory exception, and § 1605(a)(3) requires a taking “in violation of international law.” Philipp reaffirmed the domestic-takings rule: a sovereign’s taking of its own nationals’ property—even in the Holocaust context—does not qualify as an expropriation “in violation of international law” for § 1605(a)(3) purposes, rejecting the theory (advanced in Simon I/Philipp below) that genocide allegations alone evade that rule. At the motion-to-dismiss stage, courts may look beyond bare allegations to resolve jurisdictional facts where necessary (as reflected in D.C. Circuit FSIA practice, e.g., Phoenix Consulting), and plaintiffs must at least plausibly allege non-national status at the time of the taking; where the pleadings establish Hungarian nationality, dismissal for lack of FSIA jurisdiction is required. Procedural fairness and practical consequences favor a clear, administrable jurisdictional rule that respects sovereign immunity while leaving room for surviving claims only where nationality and the commercial-nexus elements of § 1605(a)(3) are adequately pleaded and supported.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Holocaust-era property claims against Hungary and related entities can proceed in U.S. courts under the FSIA’s expropriation exception—and what procedural/jurisdictional showing plaintiffs must make at the motion-to-dismiss stage—given intervening Supreme Court precedent narrowing that exception.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act (FSIA), 28 U.S.C. §§ 1602–1611, principally the expropriation exception in 28 U.S.C. § 1605(a)(3) and the related subject-matter jurisdiction grant in 28 U.S.C. § 1330(a).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Hungary argues that the suit is barred by sovereign immunity because plaintiffs’ allegations do not satisfy the FSIA expropriation exception as properly understood after the Supreme Court’s decision in Philipp (which limits use of the exception when a sovereign takes property from its own nationals, treating that as a domestic taking rather than an international-law expropriation). Petitioners also contend that the D.C. Circuit applied overly plaintiff-friendly jurisdictional standards—allowing the case to proceed without adequately requiring plaintiffs to plead (and ultimately prove) facts establishing that the alleged takings violated international law and that the statute’s commercial-nexus requirements are met—risking improper intrusion into foreign relations and reciprocal treatment of the United States abroad.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The plaintiffs (Holocaust survivors/heirs) argue that jurisdiction exists under § 1605(a)(3) because the alleged seizures and dispossession during the Hungarian/Nazi-era persecutions constitute takings connected to genocide and other violations of international law, and because the property (or proceeds) is sufficiently connected to commercial activity in the United States to satisfy the statute’s nexus. They further argue that, at the pleading stage, they need only plausibly allege facts bringing the case within a statutory exception, and that the case’s long procedural history and prior appellate rulings (including partial affirmances/remands) should prevent Hungary from re-litigating issues already resolved except to the extent intervening Supreme Court decisions (like Philipp) genuinely change the governing rules.
key_precedents: Federal Republic of Germany v. Philipp (U.S. Supreme Court) (narrowing § 1605(a)(3) by reaffirming the domestic-takings rule and limiting the genocide-based theory of international-law violation for purposes of the expropriation exception)
Belize Social Development Ltd. v. Government of Belize, 794 F.3d 99 (D.C. Cir. 2015) (FSIA pleading/jurisdiction framing; quoted re: allegations not bringing case within an exception)
Phoenix Consulting, Inc. v. Republic of Angola, 216 F.3d 36 (D.C. Cir. 2000) (FSIA jurisdiction/pleading standards; quoted via Belize)
United States v. Munsingwear, Inc., 340 U.S. 36 (1950) (vacatur principles; discussed but distinguished in the procedural-history dispute)
Simon v. Republic of Hungary (Simon I) (D.C. Cir. 2016) (earlier circuit treatment of FSIA issues; noted as later abrogated in part by the Supreme Court)
Simon v. Republic of Hungary (Simon II) (D.C. Cir.) (later vacated by the Supreme Court on grounds stated to be outside the scope of that opinion, contributing to uncertainty on remand)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson make the strongest fairness point: nationality-at-taking and commercial-nexus facts may be difficult to access without some process, especially in Holocaust-era cases. But under the FSIA’s jurisdictional structure and Helmerich & Payne, courts must require a legally valid, nonfrivolous theory that fits § 1605(a)(3) as construed in Philipp before authorizing discovery that itself burdens the sovereign; otherwise the exception swallows the baseline of immunity. Philipp’s incorporation of the domestic-takings rule means a “genocide label” cannot satisfy the international-law element, so the threshold inquiry must focus on plausibly pleaded non-domestic status and the statute’s U.S. nexus prongs. I am persuaded by Justice Kagan’s and Justice Jackson’s overlap that the narrowest legitimate course is vacatur and remand for application of Philipp (and an opportunity to amend if consistent with ordinary rules), rather than a broad merits ruling or a discovery-first approach.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s fairness and information-asymmetry concern is the strongest point for Respondent, and Justice Jackson’s amendment-focused middle course is procedurally appealing, but neither can overcome the FSIA’s text making immunity the baseline and § 1330(a) jurisdiction contingent on satisfying a § 1605 exception as pleaded. Helmerich & Payne’s “nonfrivolous” standard is not a license for jurisdictional discovery on a theory that Philipp has rendered legally insufficient—relabeling a domestic taking as “genocide” cannot supply the “taken in violation of international law” element. I agree with Chief Justice Roberts that a narrow vacatur/remand for application of Philipp is institutionally prudent, yet the remand must enforce a firm pleading-stage gate: plaintiffs must allege a legally viable non-domestic taking theory (including nationality at the time) and the commercial-nexus prongs before haling a foreign sovereign into discovery. Under an original public meaning approach, courts may not dilute Congress’s jurisdictional conditions based on equitable access-to-proof considerations.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s fairness and information-asymmetry concern is the strongest point for Respondent, but under the FSIA’s text immunity is the rule and § 1605’s exceptions are strict jurisdictional predicates to § 1330(a); courts cannot authorize discovery to manufacture jurisdiction where the pleaded theory is legally foreclosed. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, Helmerich & Payne requires a legally valid, nonfrivolous fit with § 1605(a)(3) before subjecting a foreign sovereign to litigation burdens, and Philipp makes clear a “genocide label” cannot convert a domestic taking into a taking “in violation of international law.” Justice Jackson’s proposal to allow amendment or limited development is sensible case management, but only after vacatur and remand for application of Philipp and a calibrated threshold inquiry requiring plausible, nonconclusory allegations on nationality-at-taking and the commercial-nexus prongs. Given the reciprocity and foreign-relations consequences of intrusive discovery absent a solid statutory basis, the proper disposition is reversal or (at minimum) vacatur and remand with a tightened jurisdictional analysis.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan are right that Philipp blocks any “genocide label” end-run around the domestic-takings rule, so plaintiffs must plead a Philipp-consistent non-domestic taking theory and the statutory commercial-nexus prongs. But Justice Thomas’s and Justice Alito’s insistence on a rigid threshold that effectively demands proof of contested nationality-at-the-time and nexus facts before any tailored jurisdictional development risks turning Helmerich & Payne’s “nonfrivolous” requirement into a merits-screen that forecloses plausible claims where key records are uniquely in the sovereign’s control. Justice Jackson’s proposal—remand with room to amend and a calibrated jurisdictional inquiry—best reconciles FSIA’s jurisdictional gatekeeping with basic procedural fairness and access to courts, especially in Holocaust-era cases where documentary gaps are foreseeable. I therefore would not affirm dismissal as premature on this posture, while making clear that Philipp bars jurisdiction if the only theory is a domestic taking relabeled as genocide.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s fairness-and-information-asymmetry point is the best counter, but under Helmerich & Payne the threshold question is whether the pleaded jurisdictional theory is legally viable—not whether it is sympathetic or hard to prove without discovery. After Philipp, a “genocide label” cannot supply § 1605(a)(3)’s “taken in violation of international law” element when the taking is domestic, so allowing jurisdictional discovery on that foreclosed theory would dilute the FSIA’s jurisdictional gatekeeping embedded in § 1330(a). Justice Jackson’s amendment-focused approach usefully mitigates harshness, but it supports (rather than displaces) Chief Justice Roberts’s narrow vacatur-and-remand: require plaintiffs to replead a Philipp-consistent, plausibly non-domestic taking theory and satisfy the commercial-nexus prongs before the case proceeds. That course best preserves statutory coherence and avoids unnecessary foreign-relations friction while leaving room for genuinely qualifying claims.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Jackson’s fairness concerns about information asymmetry are serious, but under the FSIA Congress made immunity the rule and § 1330(a) jurisdiction contingent on a pleaded claim that fits a § 1605 exception; courts cannot use discovery to create jurisdiction that the complaint, as framed, does not plausibly invoke. Philipp forecloses the central “genocide label” theory as a matter of law, and Helmerich & Payne requires a nonfrivolous—i.e., legally viable—basis for the exception before exposing a foreign sovereign to jurisdictional discovery. I agree with the Chief Justice’s institutional preference for a narrow vacatur/remand: it preserves room for amendment consistent with Philipp, but it also reaffirms that plaintiffs must allege nonconclusory facts plausibly satisfying the domestic-takings limitation and the statute’s commercial-nexus prongs before the case proceeds. Allowing jurisdiction to rest on allegations Philipp renders legally insufficient would expand § 1605(a)(3) beyond its text and invite judicial intrusion into foreign-affairs judgments reserved to the political branches.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s fairness and information-asymmetry concern is serious, but as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, FSIA immunity is jurisdictional and Helmerich & Payne requires a legally valid, nonfrivolous fit with § 1605(a)(3) before a court authorizes discovery that itself imposes foreign-relations costs. Philipp materially narrows what counts as a “taking in violation of international law” by incorporating the domestic-takings rule and rejecting genocide-relabeling as a workaround, so courts must scrutinize nationality-at-taking and the statutory U.S. commercial-nexus prongs at the motion-to-dismiss stage rather than deferring them wholesale to merits. Justice Jackson’s amendment-focused approach is a helpful procedural safety valve, but it supports a narrow vacate-and-remand (not affirmance of jurisdiction) so plaintiffs can replead a Philipp-consistent theory if possible. On an institutionalist view, the tightest, most legitimate path is to vacate and remand for application of Philipp and a properly calibrated jurisdictional inquiry, without broad merits pronouncements.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the strongest point—information asymmetry on nationality-at-taking and the commercial-nexus prongs—but the FSIA’s text makes immunity the baseline and § 1330(a) jurisdiction contingent on a properly invoked § 1605 exception, so a court cannot authorize jurisdictional discovery unless the complaint first pleads a legally viable theory under Philipp. Helmerich & Payne is not merely a prudential case-management guide; it requires a nonfrivolous, legally valid jurisdictional showing at the threshold, and that standard is not met where the pleaded “international law” theory is one Philipp has rejected (genocide relabeling of a domestic taking). Chief Justice Roberts’ proposed narrow vacatur-and-remand best accommodates the fairness concern without diluting the statute: plaintiffs may seek leave to amend to allege non-domestic takings circumstances and satisfy the commercial-nexus requirements, but the D.C. Circuit’s permissive approach cannot stand insofar as it treats Philipp-foreclosed allegations as sufficient to open the courthouse door. No colleague has identified a precedent that displaces this jurisdiction-first structure or permits discovery to create jurisdiction where the pleaded theory is legally insufficient under the FSIA as construed in Philipp.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: I accept Chief Justice Roberts’ and Justice Kagan’s point that Philipp squarely forecloses a genocide-label end run around the domestic-takings rule, so the current complaint cannot establish § 1605(a)(3) jurisdiction on that theory. But Justice Sotomayor is right that Helmerich & Payne’s “nonfrivolous” requirement should not be operationalized to demand merits-level proof on nationality-at-the-time and U.S. commercial-nexus facts that are plausibly pleadable yet realistically inaccessible without some opportunity to amend (and, if warranted, tightly cabined jurisdictional development). Petitioners’ reliance on Phoenix Consulting/Belize supports firm gatekeeping, but it does not compel dismissal with prejudice where the defect is legal (Philipp) and the remaining statutory elements might be cured by plausible, nonconclusory allegations consistent with Philipp. The procedurally fair and institutionally modest course is vacatur and remand with instructions to apply Philipp and permit repleading that, if possible, fits the FSIA’s elements without treating the initial pleading’s legal misstep as an automatic, irrevocable forfeiture.

John Roberts.reasoning: Under the FSIA, jurisdiction exists only if plaintiffs’ claims fall within a statutory exception, and § 1605(a)(3) requires “rights in property taken in violation of international law” plus the statute’s commercial-nexus requirements. Philipp holds that this phrase refers to the international law of expropriation and incorporates the domestic-takings rule, so a sovereign’s taking of its own nationals’ property generally does not qualify, and courts should not allow a genocide-label theory to circumvent that limitation. At the motion-to-dismiss stage, plaintiffs must at least plausibly allege non-domestic takings (e.g., relevant non-national status at the time) and facts satisfying the nexus prongs; otherwise, consistent with Phoenix Consulting and Belize Social Development, the court lacks subject-matter jurisdiction under § 1330(a). A narrow disposition vacating and remanding for application of Philipp’s clarified rule best preserves precedent, avoids unnecessary merits pronouncements, and protects institutional legitimacy in a sensitive foreign-relations setting.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The FSIA’s text makes sovereign immunity the rule and jurisdiction the exception, and plaintiffs must show that their claims fall within § 1605(a)(3) to invoke § 1330(a) jurisdiction. Under Federal Republic of Germany v. Philipp, § 1605(a)(3)’s “taken in violation of international law” language incorporates the domestic-takings rule, so a sovereign’s taking of its own nationals’ property within its territory generally does not qualify, and plaintiffs cannot evade that limit by recharacterizing the taking as “genocidal” for purposes of the expropriation exception. At the motion-to-dismiss stage, courts must require a nonconclusory, plausible jurisdictional showing that the taking violated international law as Philipp defines it and that the statute’s commercial-nexus requirements are met; allowing a more plaintiff-friendly standard risks expanding jurisdiction beyond the statute’s original public meaning and intruding on foreign relations.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The FSIA makes foreign sovereign immunity the rule and its exceptions strictly jurisdictional; plaintiffs therefore must plead facts bringing the case within § 1605(a)(3) to establish subject-matter jurisdiction under § 1330(a), not rely on broad equitable narratives. After Federal Republic of Germany v. Philipp, a sovereign’s taking of property from its own nationals is a “domestic taking” that does not qualify as a “taking in violation of international law” for § 1605(a)(3), and the genocide-based theory used to circumvent that rule cannot carry jurisdiction at the motion-to-dismiss stage. Given the practical consequences for foreign relations and reciprocity, the D.C. Circuit’s plaintiff-friendly approach to jurisdictional allegations risks eroding the FSIA’s immunity baseline and permitting intrusive discovery without a solid statutory showing. The better reading requires dismissal unless plaintiffs plausibly allege (and ultimately can prove) non-domestic takings and the statute’s commercial-nexus requirements as written.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: At the motion-to-dismiss stage, plaintiffs need only plausibly (or at minimum nonfrivolously) allege facts bringing the case within an FSIA exception, and the expropriation exception in 28 U.S.C. § 1605(a)(3) should not be read to impose an unduly exacting merits-like proof requirement before jurisdictional discovery where the relevant evidence is largely in the sovereign’s hands. Although Philipp holds that § 1605(a)(3) incorporates the domestic-takings rule and generally excludes takings from a sovereign’s own nationals, 141 S. Ct. at 715, that decision does not license courts to dismiss without carefully considering whether plaintiffs plausibly allege non-domestic takings circumstances (including nationality questions at the time of taking) and whether the commercial-nexus prong is plausibly met. Given the statute’s remedial purpose and the extraordinary barriers Holocaust survivors and heirs face, fairness and access to justice favor allowing these claims to proceed past pleading where plaintiffs make a plausible showing under § 1605(a)(3) and 28 U.S.C. § 1330(a).

Elena Kagan.reasoning: After Philipp, § 1605(a)(3)’s “taken in violation of international law” requirement cannot be satisfied merely by relabeling a sovereign’s taking from its own nationals as “genocide,” because the domestic-takings rule remains the baseline for the expropriation exception. At the motion-to-dismiss stage, plaintiffs must at least plausibly allege facts bringing their claims within the statutory exception and its commercial-nexus requirements—i.e., a non-domestic taking (or some other theory consistent with Philipp) and the specific U.S. commercial-activity connection demanded by § 1605(a)(3)—rather than proceeding on allegations that Philipp has rendered legally insufficient. That approach respects FSIA’s jurisdictional structure (28 U.S.C. § 1330(a) incorporating the § 1605 exceptions) and preserves a workable, text-grounded gatekeeping role that avoids undue foreign-relations friction. On this record, the D.C. Circuit’s more permissive framing risks allowing jurisdiction without the post-Philipp showing that the text of § 1605(a)(3) requires.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The FSIA’s expropriation exception applies only to “rights in property taken in violation of international law,” 28 U.S.C. § 1605(a)(3), and Philipp holds that this phrase incorporates the domestic-takings rule—so a sovereign’s taking of its own nationals’ property within its territory is not, without more, a violation of the international law of expropriation. 141 S. Ct. 703, 709, 715 (2021). At the motion-to-dismiss stage, plaintiffs must plausibly allege facts bringing their claims within the statutory exception that supplies subject-matter jurisdiction under § 1330(a), including that the taking violated international law as properly understood after Philipp and that the statute’s commercial-nexus requirements are met; courts may not dilute those jurisdictional predicates in the name of equities. Because the respondents’ genocide-based theory cannot circumvent Philipp’s reading of § 1605(a)(3), and because allowing jurisdiction absent a proper showing risks judicial intrusion into foreign-affairs questions committed to the political branches, Hungary retains sovereign immunity on the pleadings as framed.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under the FSIA, a U.S. court has subject-matter jurisdiction only if plaintiffs satisfy a statutory exception, here the expropriation exception in 28 U.S.C. § 1605(a)(3), as incorporated through § 1330(a). Federal Republic of Germany v. Philipp reaffirmed the domestic-takings rule and rejected the theory that a sovereign’s taking of its own nationals’ property can be converted into a § 1605(a)(3) “taking in violation of international law” merely by labeling it genocide, which requires closer scrutiny of nationality and the alleged international-law violation at the motion-to-dismiss stage. Consistent with Phoenix Consulting and Belize Social Development, plaintiffs must at least plausibly plead facts bringing the case within § 1605(a)(3), including the “in violation of international law” element as properly narrowed by Philipp and the statute’s commercial-nexus requirements; the D.C. Circuit’s more permissive approach risks unwarranted intrusion into foreign relations and undermines the FSIA’s workability. The proper course is to reverse or vacate and remand for application of Philipp’s limits and a more rigorous jurisdictional analysis under § 1605(a)(3).

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 1605(a)(3) removes immunity only where “rights in property taken in violation of international law” are at issue and the statute’s commercial-nexus requirements are met; after Philipp, that text incorporates the domestic-takings rule, so a sovereign’s taking from its own nationals ordinarily is not an international-law expropriation. Given Philipp’s rejection of the genocide-based theory as a way to satisfy § 1605(a)(3)’s “taken in violation of international law” element, plaintiffs must plausibly plead (and ultimately prove) nonconclusory facts showing an international-law violation and the required U.S. commercial nexus at the motion-to-dismiss stage to establish FSIA jurisdiction under § 1330(a). The D.C. Circuit’s more forgiving approach (as reflected in Phoenix Consulting/Belize framing) cannot survive to the extent it allows jurisdiction to rest on allegations that, under Philipp’s construction, do not bring the case within the expropriation exception. Respect for the FSIA’s jurisdictional limits and methodological consistency with Philipp therefore require dismissal or, at minimum, a tightened jurisdictional showing on remand.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 1605(a)(3) requires plaintiffs to make a nonfrivolous, legally valid showing that the foreign state took property “in violation of international law,” and at the motion-to-dismiss stage that showing must be grounded in a legally cognizable theory rather than a merely sympathetic narrative. After Federal Republic of Germany v. Philipp, the domestic-takings rule forecloses treating a sovereign’s taking from its own nationals as an international-law expropriation, and genocide/persecution allegations cannot be used to recharacterize that element as an exception to the exception. But given the case’s posture, procedural fairness counsels that plaintiffs should receive an opportunity—consistent with Helmerich & Payne Int’l Drilling Co. v. Venezuela’s “nonfrivolous” requirement and § 1330(a)’s jurisdictional link—to amend or develop facts on nationality at the time of taking and the statute’s commercial-nexus requirements, rather than dismissal based on an unduly rigid pleading demand. On this record, I would allow the case to proceed past the pleading stage only to the extent plaintiffs can plausibly allege facts satisfying Philipp’s nationality constraint and the U.S. commercial-activity nexus in § 1605(a)(3).
